shows.md:
Kept that line. Now the weak points — where the argument is more fragile than it first sounds:

- **"Small teams can't afford the process"** — writing 20 behavioral cases before every launch assumes headcount most startups don't have. The piece doesn't really answer this; it just shows a team that did have the time.
- **"Some behavior is only knowable in production"** — the author's own prescription (test it all up front) can't catch behavior that only emerges with real user inputs at scale. Pre-ship tests are necessarily a sample, not a proof.
Where do you land — is 'write the behavior down before you write the code' practical advice, or does it just push the cost of testing onto teams too small to pay it?

shows.md: This isn't a tooling gap — it's a habit problem. Four other AI stories are queued behind it: agents needing undo instead of confirm dialogs, voice assistants learning to hand off, time-to-first-token as the new page load, and per-seat pricing breaking for agents.

shows.title: The Eval Gap: Why AI Products Ship Without Tests
shows.why_matters: If you build AI products, this changes what you measure first.

shows.md: The real claim: teams build rigorous tests for their infrastructure — uptime, latency, API contracts — but almost never for the model's actual behavior, so the first real test of whether the AI says something wrong happens in front of a user. It's framed as a tooling gap, but the author is really indicting a habit: engineering orgs know how to test deterministic systems and haven't rebuilt that instinct for probabilistic ones.

transcript.user: Walk me through The Eval Gap.

shows.md: Watching logs does catch things no pre-ship eval would predict — real users produce inputs no test suite imagines, and that's a legitimate limit of evals. But the article's case studies aren't about exotic edge cases; they're regressions a basic behavioral check would've caught before anyone outside the team saw them. 'Watch the logs' still means the first failure lands on a real user — you've just moved the test to production and called it monitoring.

His rebuttal isn't 'build the full harness' — it's that a lightweight behavioral check costs less than the incident that skipping one causes.

"**Argument:** Teams test the plumbing (uptime, latency, schemas) but skip testing model behavior, so regressions reach real users before anyone catches them.

**My take:** Evals are overkill for a small team — ship and watch the logs."

shows.why_matters: If you build AI products, this changes what you measure first.

shows.md: The underlying claim is that SaaS pricing assumed a human bottleneck — one seat, one set of hands. Agents remove that bottleneck, so billing per seat starts charging for something that no longer limits usage. The harder question the piece leaves open: outcome-based pricing requires agreeing what an 'outcome' is, and that's rarely as clean as a seat count.
